title_en: What a Town Full of Vibecoders Says About the Chinese Economy
title_zh: 一个满是 vibe coder 的小镇，透露出中国经济的什么信号
subtitle_zh: 记者 Aphra Wong 走进“vibe coding 之都”良渚，从算命 app、AI 教育到短剧工业，透视更务实也更焦虑的中国。
summary_zh: 本集 Odd Lots 由 Joe Weisenthal 与 Tracy Alloway 主持，嘉宾是报道中国 AI 的记者 Aphra Wong，带来“AI 与中国社会”三部曲的实地观察。与美国科技界的末日焦虑不同，中国社会对 AI 更务实乐观：民调显示 83% 的中国人认为 AI 有益，美国仅 38%。中国把 AI 视为“下一个互联网”，“AI+”计划强调把技术扩散到千行百业，而非只竞速前沿模型。Wong 探访了杭州郊外的“vibe coding 之都”良渚：租金低廉、生活悠闲，聚集了大量逃离 996、拒绝主流科技圈的一人公司（OPC）和年轻 vibe coder，做算命、ADHD、心理健康等应用，其中 AI 算命 app FateTel 是少数真正赚钱的。她还调查了缺乏监管的 AI 教育产业，如“生财有术”这类近乎传销、贩卖希望的公司，以及地方政府一哄而上造成的 AIGC“鬼城”——90% 的 AIGC 公司在亏钱，只有 0.16% 的内容成为爆款。Wong 认为疫情后中国已变成低信任、零和的社会，经济“日本化”停滞，官方青年失业率 18.9%。还谈到审查与周期性产能过剩。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Lots podcast. I'm Joe Wiesenthal.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: So, Trace, we at this point, obviously, we've done a fair amount of episodes about AI in China.
turns.zh: Trace，到现在为止，显然我们已经做了不少关于中国 AI 的节目。

turns.en: Oh, OK. It's like a fair amount.
turns.zh: 哦，好吧，算是不少。

turns.en: Yeah, obviously.
turns.zh: 是啊，显然。

turns.en: We've done a lot of episodes about AI. We've done a little bit about AI in China. Like one of the things, and it's like very, there's a lot to learn still. But, you know, one of the things, and it sort of maybe even precedes AI a little bit, but seems to be continuing, is that at least in the U.S. tech world, for several years now, and AI specifically, we just, there's this dread, there's this fears of dystopia, the sort of end of the world type stuff. It all comes up part of the package, right? And one of the things we know from various conversations we've had, you know, talking to people in China about tech in general, is that tech in general is not viewed the same way as sort of like big tech in the US has come in terms of like deeply negative things. But then also the other thing is that all these sort of end of the world hypotheses that the AI people love to talk about, you get the vibe that it's a little more pragmatic and normal when they talk about these things in China. The less weird it is.
turns.zh: 我们做过很多关于 AI 的节目，也做过一点关于中国 AI 的内容。有一点——当然还有很多要学的——而且这一点甚至可能在 AI 之前就存在了，但似乎一直在延续：至少在美国科技界，这几年，尤其是谈到 AI 时，总有一种恐惧，一种对反乌托邦、对世界末日般结局的担忧，这些仿佛都是配套出现的一部分，对吧？我们从跟中国科技界人士的各种交流中了解到的一点是，总体而言，科技在中国并不像美国大型科技公司那样被赋予那么多负面的意味。另外还有一点，那些 AI 圈的人特别爱谈的末日假说，你会感觉到，在中国人们谈论这些事情时会更务实、更平常心一些，没那么古怪。

turns.en: I mean, well, weird in another way.
turns.zh: 我是说，嗯，是另一种意义上的古怪。

turns.en: Maybe weird in another way, but you know. Not in the Silicon Valley way. Not in the Berkeley way.
turns.zh: 也许是另一种古怪，但你知道，不是硅谷那种，也不是伯克利那种。

turns.en: China has, oh, no one's weird in the Berkeley way except Berkeley. China has a history of, I guess, embracing new technologies, at least like in recent decades, right? Because that is seen as the driving force of economic progress and economic progress is part of the, I guess, bargain that the CCP has made. with its domestic population. So I think there is a pragmatism there. One thing I would say, though, is the technology that they embrace can change very quickly. And we saw that when they started cracking down on a lot of the software and internet companies and the disappearance of Jack Ma and things like that. What's happening now that I think is really interesting is the government has basically told everyone to embrace AI in various ways. And the way they're doing it seems kind of different to the U.S., obviously. But in the U.S., it seems much more about developing the frontier models. In China, it seems much more about not just developing cheaper open source models, but also diffusing the technology through the economy.
turns.zh: 说到伯克利式的古怪，除了伯克利自己，没人那么古怪。中国有一段——我想说——拥抱新技术的历史，至少近几十年是这样，对吧？因为这被视为经济进步的驱动力，而经济进步又是中国共产党（CCP）与国内民众之间某种契约的一部分。所以我觉得这里面有一种务实。不过我要说的是，他们拥抱的技术可以变得很快。我们看到，当他们开始打压很多软件和互联网公司、以及马云（Jack Ma）消失等事情发生时就是如此。我觉得现在真正有意思的是，政府基本上是让所有人都以各种方式去拥抱 AI。他们的做法显然跟美国不太一样。在美国，重点更多是开发前沿模型；而在中国，重点似乎不只是开发更便宜的开源模型，还包括把这项技术扩散到整个经济当中。

turns.en: Totally. I've said it on the podcast before, so it's not new. I'm an avid consumer of Chinese propaganda online.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我在播客里以前就说过，所以不算新鲜。我是中国网络宣传内容的忠实消费者。

turns.en: I'm sorry, Joe's China maxing.
turns.zh: 抱歉，Joe 这是在“China maxing”（沉浸式刷中国内容）。

turns.en: No, I just like, my Instagram reels are just like, here's this incredible machine to peel shrimp or buy our machine to make toilet paper in your home or something like that from all these hundreds of companies, manufacturing companies. Like, I'm an eager consumer of Chinese industrial propaganda. But like one of those stories that was going around, they're like, oh. All these old, like, grandmothers are really getting into open claw and stuff like that. Remember those stories? And I was like, is that real? And I was like, come on.
turns.zh: 没有啦，我只是——我的 Instagram reels 全是这种：看这台神奇的剥虾机，或者买我们这台能在家造卫生纸的机器之类的，来自成百上千家制造企业。我就是中国工业宣传的热心观众。不过之前流传的一个故事说，哦，所有那些老奶奶都迷上了 open claw 之类的东西。还记得那些报道吗？我当时就想，这是真的假的？得了吧。

turns.en: Oh, you know what I saw on the subway yesterday? There was an old lady who sat next to me, a Western lady, and she was on her phone and she was watching some sort of AI generated soap opera. And I had never seen one of these before. It had like sort of anime looking characters, but they were clearly AI generated talking about it was like a woman working in an office building and she was like getting engaged to some other guy. It looks ridiculous. I'd never seen that before, but people are clearly watching it.
turns.zh: 哦，你知道我昨天在地铁上看到什么吗？有位老太太坐在我旁边，是位西方女士，她在看手机，正在看某种 AI 生成的肥皂剧。我以前从没见过这种东西。里面是那种看着像动漫的角色，但明显是 AI 生成的，讲的是一个在写字楼上班的女人，她好像要跟另一个男人订婚了。看起来特别离谱。我以前从没见过，但显然有人在看。

turns.en: So bleak. Anyway, let's talk about actual people, what's going on. I'm very excited to say we really do have the perfect guest. Someone who has been doing some really original reporting on this that could talk about AI in China more than just like the race, unquote. We're going to be speaking with Aphra Wong. She is a writer, reporter covering AI in China and Silicon Valley. Recently had some great pieces published in New Yorker, New York Mag, so forth. So, Aphra, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.
turns.zh: 太荒诞了。好了，我们来聊聊真实的人和真实的情况吧。我非常高兴地说，我们真的请到了完美的嘉宾。有人在就此做非常原创的报道，能谈论中国的 AI，而不只是所谓的“竞赛”。我们将要和 Aphra Wong 对话。她是一位作家、记者，报道中国的 AI 和硅谷，最近在 New Yorker、New York Mag 等刊物上发表了一些很棒的文章。Aphra，非常感谢你来上我们的播客。

turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。

turns.en: Bunch of people love your reporting.
turns.zh: 很多人都喜欢你的报道。

turns.en: It's fresh. It's new.
turns.zh: 很新鲜，很新。

turns.en: What do you set out to cover? What's your beat?
turns.zh: 你一开始想报道什么？你的报道领域是什么？

turns.en: So recently I published three pieces, what I call the trilogy of AI and the Chinese society. I think it has a common thread of what is the AI diffusing story in China, like how people perceive the AI plus plan, how people perceive AI as being held as the high quality productivity force, right? You know, announced by Xi Jinping. So I'm trying to like really understand the individual stories in China, like How do vibe coders understand this technology? How do the regular tech workers understand this technology? How do they really jump on this technology? on this bus to push this technology forward, like in a sense, create a really unique Chinese AI topology and those communities. So I was visiting China's vibe coding capital, which is a city near Hangzhou. I was researching and investigating this lucrative AI education industry in China, which is a newly emerged industry after the deep seek boom. And then I was also sort of investigating the AI sloths, like, you know, Tracy, you saw on the subway, like where do those AI dramas created.
turns.zh: 最近我发表了三篇文章，我称之为“AI 与中国社会”三部曲。我觉得它们有一条共同的主线，就是 AI 在中国扩散的故事：人们如何看待“AI+”（AI plus）计划，如何看待 AI 被定位为“高质量生产力”——你知道，这是习近平提出的说法。所以我努力去真正理解中国的个体故事：vibe coder（氛围编程者）如何理解这项技术？普通科技从业者如何理解它？他们又是如何真正跳上这趟技术快车、推动这项技术向前，某种意义上创造出一种非常独特的中国 AI 生态和社群的？我去探访了中国的 vibe coding 之都，那是杭州附近的一座城市。我调研并调查了中国这个利润丰厚的 AI 教育产业，这是 DeepSeek 热潮之后新兴的行业。我还调查了 AI slop（AI 垃圾内容），就是 Tracy 你在地铁上看到的那种，那些 AI 剧到底是在哪里造出来的。

turns.en: And why are people watching them? That's my big question.
turns.zh: 还有人们为什么要看这些东西？这是我最大的疑问。

turns.en: Well, it is because humans are stupid. We're psychologically hacked by those AI slot machines really know how to hack our brain. Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，因为人类很蠢。我们在心理上被那些 AI 老虎机黑了，它们真的很懂得如何黑进我们的大脑。是的。

turns.en: Yeah. I have so many questions already. But before we drill down into some of your on the ground reporting, can you just talk to us about the AI plus program? And what is it exactly that China's authorities have said they want to achieve here?
turns.zh: 是啊，我已经有一大堆问题了。不过在我们深入你的实地报道之前，你能先跟我们讲讲“AI+”计划吗？中国官方到底说想通过它实现什么？

turns.en: Yeah, the conventional wisdom that's perceived by the U.S. tech industry is that China emphasizes more on AI diffusion. And one sign is that Xi Jinping himself, for example, in all his public speeches, he only mentioned things like AI plus or AI as the highest quality productivity force, which is a very Marxist term. What China wants is really use AI to empower thousands of industries like manufacturing and like supply chains and the state who really want to diffuse this technology. And similar to what internet did to China 10, 20 years ago, where China successfully established the e-commerce business, for example, China has successfully incubated many successful mobile internet companies like ByteDance, the creator of TikTok. So China sees AI as the next internet So the AI plus plan is really similar to the previous internet plus plan, which is AI plus factory or AI plus education or AI plus agriculture. So many people, entrepreneurs and tech workers I met, they're all like trying to think about how to actually materialize AI, like bring AI to their unique business, to their unique verticals.
turns.zh: 是的，美国科技界的普遍看法是，中国更强调 AI 的扩散。一个迹象是，习近平本人在他所有的公开讲话中，只提到“AI+”，或者把 AI 称为“最高质量的生产力”——这是个很马克思主义的说法。中国真正想做的，是用 AI 赋能制造业、供应链等成千上万的行业，而国家也真的很想扩散这项技术。这类似于 10 年、20 年前互联网对中国所做的事——当时中国成功建立了电商业务，成功孵化出很多移动互联网公司，比如 TikTok 的母公司 ByteDance（字节跳动）。所以中国把 AI 看作下一个互联网。“AI+”计划其实和之前的“互联网+”计划很像，就是 AI+工厂、AI+教育、AI+农业。我遇到的很多创业者、科技从业者都在琢磨怎么把 AI 真正落地，把 AI 带到他们独特的业务、他们独特的垂直领域里去。

turns.en: We met at a conference at Berkeley a few weeks ago, which was what Curve, and that was like, again, what people call like, there are a lot of doomers there. And these people were like very worried that in a short period of time, you know, you can pick which flavor of it you want, but bad things will happen. And there was this conversation that sometimes comes up like, when will China wake up to the risk of AGI? And you see people talk about this publicly. You hear people talk about this privately as if, and I don't know whether it's like as if People just think like Chinese leadership is very stupid about the risks or as if perhaps like maybe if they were as like, quote, AGI pulled as these people are that that would per se mean they would be posting online about it more like they are. When you hear these questions, when will they wake up about AGI? What's your response? What's your thought there?
turns.zh: 几周前我们在伯克利的一个会议上碰过面，那个会叫 What Curve（音），同样，用人们的话说，那儿有很多末日论者（doomer）。这些人非常担心，在很短的时间内——你可以选你喜欢的任何一种说法——坏事会发生。有一个话题时不时会冒出来：中国什么时候才会醒悟到 AGI（通用人工智能）的风险？你会看到有人公开谈论这个，也会听到有人私下谈论，就好像——我不知道是不是——大家觉得中国领导层对风险很无知，又或者，如果他们也像这些人一样“AGI 上头”，那他们本身就会像这些人一样在网上多发这类帖子。当你听到“他们什么时候才会对 AGI 醒悟过来”这种问题时，你会怎么回应？你怎么看？

turns.en: Okay, so the.
turns.zh: 好的，所以说。

turns.en: Version of me you're talking to right now is a new me. I actually went through something called RSI psychosis, which I was pretty much convinced by today's progress of RSI in a sense of fully automated self-recursive improving loop. And to me, today's trajectory, especially the frontier labs that the US labs are doing, has a reasonable and predictable curve. It is an exponential curve. And I do think a similar curve might happen in China now. Speaking from someone who is really RSI-pilled, I think China has yet to wake up.
turns.zh: 你现在对话的这个版本的我，是一个全新的我。我其实经历过一种叫“RSI 精神病”（RSI psychosis）的状态——我几乎被如今 RSI（递归自我改进）的进展说服了，也就是那种全自动的、自我递归改进的循环。对我来说，今天的轨迹，尤其是美国前沿实验室正在做的事情，有一条合理且可预测的曲线，那是一条指数曲线。我确实认为类似的曲线现在也可能在中国发生。作为一个真正“RSI 上头”的人，我觉得中国还没有醒悟过来。

turns.en: So you agree with this? Actually, that basic thing is like, yeah, they should probably wake up about this.
turns.zh: 所以你同意这个说法？其实那个基本的点是，是啊，他们大概应该对这件事醒悟过来。

turns.en: Right. Actually, in a sense, I do agree with you. I do think China has not filled the AGI yet. I'm quoting Ilya Soskever here. It's like, fill the AGI. It might soon. But now I would also argue that the AI race that China is participating in is a full-stack race. It is a race that involves the amount of electricity it generates. It involves all sorts of the entire AI supply chain rather than just racing to the frontier AI. So I think China is running in a race where U.S. has not really fully signed up for.
turns.zh: 对。其实某种意义上，我确实同意你的说法。我确实认为中国还没有“感受到 AGI”（fill the AGI）——我这里引用 Ilya Sutskever 的话，就是“感受到 AGI”，这种感觉可能很快会来。但现在我还要说，中国参与的这场 AI 竞赛是一场全栈竞赛，它涉及发电量，涉及整条 AI 供应链的方方面面，而不只是竞速前沿 AI。所以我觉得中国正在跑的这场竞赛，是美国其实还没有完全投入的那一场。

turns.en: And U.S.
turns.zh: 而美国。

turns.en: Is running an AI race that China hasn't fully signed up for. So, like, both countries are running on their own race and interpreting this competition in different ways. Hmm.
turns.zh: 正在跑一场中国还没有完全投入的 AI 竞赛。所以，两国其实都在跑各自的竞赛，用不同的方式解读这场竞争。嗯。

turns.en: This might be a weird question, but is one of the reasons that China, I mean, China is catching up on a lot of the frontier models, at least if you look at various benchmarks, but it started out slower than the U.S., obviously. How does the actual Chinese language play into the development of LLMs? Because, I mean, I remember like just trying to type. Chinese characters on a phone can be very challenging depending on what system you use and whether you use like pinyin or something like that. But is that an obstacle to LLMs?
turns.zh: 这可能是个奇怪的问题，但中国在很多前沿模型上正在追赶——至少从各种基准测试来看是这样——不过它起步显然比美国慢。中文本身在 LLM（大语言模型）的开发中扮演什么角色？因为我记得，光是想在手机上输入汉字就可能很有挑战性，取决于你用什么系统、用不用拼音之类的。这对 LLM 来说是个障碍吗？

turns.en: Yeah. It reminds me of two, three years ago when DeepSeq R1 seems came out of nowhere. It became the first, this original Chinese large language model that's welcomed by the entire Chinese society because DeepSeq R1 is pre-trained with a lot of original Chinese texts that they crawled online. Before, Chinese people only had the options of hopping up on a VPN and use ChatGPT or Cloud, where the language itself feels really translated and foreign. And DeepSeq R1 is the first native large language model that people start to develop a kinship or develop some attachment to. It's a little bit like ChaiGPT-03, which is the large language world that's really symphonic and become lovers of many people. But I think R1s played that role during the initial wave of the Chinese AI.
turns.zh: 是的。这让我想起两三年前，DeepSeek R1 仿佛横空出世。它是第一个受到整个中国社会欢迎的原生中文大语言模型，因为 DeepSeek R1 用了大量从网上爬取的原生中文文本进行预训练。在此之前，中国人只能靠翻 VPN 去用 ChatGPT 或 Claude，那种语言本身感觉很“翻译腔”、很外来。而 DeepSeek R1 是第一个让人们开始产生亲近感、产生某种情感依附的原生大语言模型。它有点像 ChatGPT-03（音），那个大语言模型曾经非常有共鸣感，成了很多人的心头好。我觉得 R1 在中国 AI 的第一波浪潮中就扮演了那样的角色。

turns.en: So obviously ChaiGPT, you could use it in Chinese, but it was what was distinct for China about DeepSeek, besides it being Chinese, is that having been trained on a lot of Chinese tech specifically... It felt like reading actual Chinese as opposed to maybe like English translated into Chinese or something like that.
turns.zh: 显然 ChatGPT 你也能用中文，但 DeepSeek 对中国来说与众不同的地方，除了它是中文的，还在于它是专门用大量中文文本训练出来的……感觉就像在读真正的中文，而不是像英文翻译成中文那种。

turns.en: Yeah, many people were really shocked by the philosophical depth that Deep Seek R1 showed two years ago. You was able to easily pull some verses from Tang Dynasty and, you know, give people really graceful and beautiful answers. And people just genuinely feel like, wow, there's a Chinese AI that's available to us. To note that before Deep Seek, the Chinese industry actually had an ego death moment, simply because China was experiencing deflation. There's post-COVID dread. Chinese economy wasn't doing really well. And at the same time, the Silicon Valley people, they figure out something like Chai GPT. It's like the coming to Jesus moment for many people. But like, what do we have in China, right? So At the time, a lot of the Chinese tech people that I know are all posting a bunch of social media posts saying, China cannot innovate. There's no way we can catch up with this chat GPT moment anymore. And then Deep Seat came out. And then it is, at the time, was seen as a sign for national destiny. In Chinese, it's called guoyun. It's actually a terminology that Xi Jinping often used. People truly believe that The emergence of ChaiGPT, the sheer existence of ChaiGPT is an indicator that China is a prosperous and a lucky nation that has talent like Liang Wenfeng. It's, you know, a hidden gem doing quants and then later decided to buy a bunch of GPUs and decided to train Chinese own models.
turns.zh: 是的，两年前 DeepSeek R1 展现出的哲学深度让很多人震惊。你能轻松地让它引出一些唐代的诗句，给出非常优雅、优美的回答。人们真切地感到，哇，有一个属于我们中国人自己的 AI 可用了。要知道，在 DeepSeek 之前，中国科技行业其实经历过一次“自我崩塌”（ego death）的时刻，仅仅因为当时中国正经历通缩，有疫情后的低迷，中国经济表现得不太好。与此同时，硅谷的人搞出了 ChatGPT 这样的东西，对很多人来说那是个“幡然醒悟”的时刻。可我们中国有什么呢？所以当时我认识的很多中国科技人都在社交媒体上发一堆帖子说，中国没法创新，我们再也不可能追上这个 ChatGPT 时刻了。然后 DeepSeek 出来了。在当时，它被视为国家命运的征兆，中文里叫“国运”，这其实是习近平经常用的一个词。人们真的相信，DeepSeek 的出现、DeepSeek 本身的存在，就说明中国是一个繁荣而幸运的国家，拥有像梁文锋（Liang Wenfeng）这样的人才。他是块隐藏的璞玉，本来做量化，后来决定买一大堆 GPU，决定训练中国自己的模型。

turns.en: Okay, so deep seek is the sort of moment when a lot of people get excited about AI in China. Let me ask a basic question first. Why do they seem to be more excited about AI than a lot of people here in the West? I don't want to talk in generalities. I am talking in generalities. Obviously, there are exceptions on both sides of the ocean, but just why in general does it seem like Chinese people seem to be embracing AI or at least experimenting with it.
turns.zh: 好的，所以 DeepSeek 是很多人开始对中国 AI 感到兴奋的那个时刻。我先问个基础问题：为什么他们看起来比西方这里的很多人对 AI 更兴奋？我不想泛泛而谈——好吧我就是在泛泛而谈。显然两岸都有例外，但总体而言，为什么中国人似乎在拥抱 AI，或者至少愿意去尝试它？

turns.en: Yes. So the polling data actually indicates that there are 83% of Chinese people believe that AI would be beneficial to their life and work. In contrast, the number in the U.S. is 38, which means U.S. is much more pessimistic about AI itself. And I think there are a few reasons why the Chinese society and Chinese people seem to in a sense, radically embracing AI, the first reason is what choice do they have, right? Can they say no to this technology? There is no meaningful collective or public organized demonstration to meaningfully say no to this technology. And if you live in a Chinese society, it is really easy to buy this totality of this historical view that China is heading towards a direction and then In this direction, AI is waiting for us. AI is going to help China to upgrade its industry. It is, in a sense, like a Darwinian or inevitable trend that you have to participate. So I think one reason why people, in a sense, feeling optimistic about AI is because they really don't have a choice. It's a result of joylessness. And the second reason is, in the past, China has been through a few industrial upgrading cycles. And the people's life are visibly improved by those changes. One story I really like to tell is the story of my grandma. She is 81 years old now. In the 80s, she is a woman who lives in rural Shandong. It is a time where she needed to walk for five hours to buy a clock for her kids because her kids needed to check time to go to school on time. And now my grandma is addicted to her Xiaomi smartphone. My grandma, you know, she brought this voice control smart light bulbs. And she loves using her voice to command the light bulb to change colors and turn it on and off. And she's also chatting with Doubao all the time, which is China's most popular chatbot. So for my grandma, she's very optimistic and looking forward to the future. It's simply because the economic rising and the technological changes are intertwined together. And the benefits of those technology has been enormous to Chinese people's normal life.
turns.zh: 是的。民调数据其实显示，有 83% 的中国人相信 AI 会给他们的生活和工作带来好处。相比之下，美国的这个数字是 38%，也就是说美国对 AI 本身要悲观得多。我觉得中国社会和中国人之所以某种意义上在激进地拥抱 AI，有几个原因。第一个原因是，他们有别的选择吗？他们能对这项技术说不吗？并没有真正意义上的集体或公开组织的示威来对这项技术说不。如果你生活在中国社会，你很容易就会全盘接受这种历史观：中国正朝着某个方向前进，而在那个方向上，AI 在等着我们，AI 会帮助中国升级产业。这在某种意义上是一种达尔文式的、不可逆转的趋势，你必须参与。所以我觉得人们对 AI 感到乐观的一个原因，恰恰是因为他们真的别无选择，这是一种“没有愉悦感”的结果。第二个原因是，过去中国经历过几轮产业升级周期，人们的生活被这些变化肉眼可见地改善了。我特别喜欢讲的一个故事是我奶奶的故事。她现在 81 岁了。80 年代，她是一个住在山东农村的女人。那时候她需要走五个小时的路去给孩子买一个钟，因为孩子得看时间才能准时上学。而现在，我奶奶迷上了她的小米（Xiaomi）智能手机。她还买了语音控制的智能灯泡，特别喜欢用语音命令灯泡变换颜色、开关。她还一直在跟豆包（Doubao）聊天，那是中国最受欢迎的聊天机器人。所以对我奶奶来说，她非常乐观、非常期待未来，仅仅是因为经济崛起和技术变革是交织在一起的，而这些技术给中国人的日常生活带来的好处是巨大的。

turns.en: That makes a lot of sense. So you wrote this piece. You said something that I want to go back to now. China's vibe coding capital. And you wrote about that for The New Yorker. And in that piece, you talk a lot about this company that built an ad powered fortune telling app. And there's like, when I hear, like when I read that story and when I hear something like the term Chinese vibe coding capital, there's a lot in there that it's just like a rich thing in terms of what I think about. Like for one, it's very hard to imagine in the US another exciting tech city besides San Francisco and maybe San Francisco and New York. Like we don't have like another thing right now so it's like booming industries intensely concentrated which we know is very different like China's multiple booming tech cities all at the same time so I find that interesting I find it interesting that like okay there are these people who want to do tech stuff but don't want to be part of like some big company grind the 996 stuff that we've heard about and then I find it interesting that by fortune telling that like this is something that we associate with like China for a really long time that like long before AI is a country or culture is into horoscopes and fortune telling and all that stuff. It really seems like a lot of things coming together with this story.
turns.zh: 这很有道理。你写了这篇文章，里面有个说法我想现在回过头来聊聊：中国的 vibe coding 之都。你为 New Yorker 写了这个。在那篇文章里，你大量谈到一家做了一款靠广告盈利的算命 app 的公司。当我读到这个故事、当我听到“中国 vibe coding 之都”这样的词时，里面有太多东西让我浮想联翩。首先，在美国，除了旧金山、也许旧金山和纽约之外，很难想象还有另一个激动人心的科技城市。我们现在没有别的这样的地方，所以这种“蓬勃产业高度集中”的情况，跟中国同时有多个蓬勃发展的科技城市是很不一样的，我觉得这很有意思。我觉得有意思的是，有一群人想做科技，但不想成为那种大公司苦活儿、我们听说过的“996”的一部分。然后我觉得有意思的是，算命这件事——这是我们长期以来跟中国联系在一起的东西，早在 AI 之前，这个国家或文化就热衷星座、算命之类。这个故事真的像是很多东西汇聚到了一起。

turns.en: Yeah. This one charming thing about this vibe-coding town, to give a little bit of context, it is a small town that sits outskirt of Hangzhou. Hangzhou is China's tech hub. That's where DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Unitree is in. And this vibe-coding capital called Liangzhu is 20, 30 minutes from Hangzhou. And this town is just charming and beautiful. The name itself, Liangzhu, it means beautiful waterland. And it really earns a name because if you go there, there's a lot of green grass, there's marshes, there's lakes, there's rivers, and there are a lot of low-rise buildings. The lifestyle in Liangzhu is really chill. And at the same time, Liangzhu has a cheap rental market and the housing price is relatively cheap. So many better tech workers, they either got laid off from big tech or they're really tired of the 996 grand game. they would leave a city like Beijing and Shanghai, which is way too competitive and way too expensive to live in, and then move to Liangzhu to start something on their own with AI. So you see a lot of OPCs there, one-person companies. You see a lot of just like independent vibe coders there. You see a lot of young people who don't even bother to find a job. They just, after graduating, they're tech savvy enough, they just directly move to Liangzhu. So there's a A congregation of those people in the recent years come to this vibe coding capital and start their own businesses. And the kind of businesses or the product they built are not necessarily the super apps like WeChat or Alipay, where you can do everything with those apps. So the applications the Liangzhu people are building are quirky, whimsical, and interesting. So there's a fortune-telling app that I discovered recently. And then there are people who are building applications just for ADHD people or people with dyslexia. There are a lot of people who are building apps for mental health, mental well-being. There are many people building apps to help you to focus. It's about productivity. So these are the group of people who actively refusing to participate in the mainstream tech scene in China. And then they kind of vote with their feet. It was like they chose to go to Liangzhu and live a different lifestyle. In Liangzhu, like you can both lay flat, it means be a little bit more like a slacker, you know, don't really do anything. Or you can participate in some entrepreneurial stuff. Like Liangzhu is a place that allows all those lifestyle to exist.
turns.zh: 是的。这个 vibe coding 小镇有一个很迷人的地方。给点背景：它是位于杭州郊外的一座小镇。杭州是中国的科技中心，DeepSeek、Alibaba（阿里巴巴）、Unitree（宇树）都在那儿。这个叫良渚（Liangzhu）的 vibe coding 之都离杭州二三十分钟车程。这座小镇非常迷人、非常美。名字本身“良渚”就意味着美丽的水乡，它也名副其实，因为你去到那儿，会看到大片绿草、沼泽、湖泊、河流，还有很多低层建筑。良渚的生活节奏非常悠闲。同时，良渚的租房市场很便宜，房价也相对较低。所以很多科技从业者，要么是从大厂被裁，要么是实在厌倦了 996 那种苦活儿，他们会离开北京、上海这种竞争太激烈、生活成本太高的城市，搬到良渚，用 AI 自己创业。所以你会看到很多 OPC（一人公司），很多独立的 vibe coder，还有很多年轻人甚至懒得找工作，毕业后因为足够懂技术，直接搬到良渚。近几年有这样一群人聚集到这个 vibe coding 之都，创办自己的事业。他们做的产品不一定是像微信（WeChat）或支付宝（Alipay）那种什么都能干的超级 app。良渚的人做的应用古灵精怪、异想天开、有意思。比如我最近发现的一款算命 app，还有人在专门给 ADHD（多动症）人群或阅读障碍人群做应用，很多人做心理健康、精神福祉类的 app，很多人做帮你专注的 app，讲效率。这些人主动拒绝参与中国主流的科技圈，算是用脚投票——他们选择去良渚，过一种不一样的生活。在良渚，你既可以“躺平”，就是当个稍微懒散一点的人，什么都不太干；也可以参与一些创业的事情。良渚是一个能让所有这些生活方式共存的地方。

turns.en: So I- It was like Austin 25 years ago, but it's not the case anymore.
turns.zh: 所以——它就像 25 年前的 Austin（奥斯汀），但现在 Austin 已经不是那样了。

turns.en: Yeah, sadly. So I met, yeah, the founder of this AI astrology app called FateTel. And he is someone who 10 years ago, he wanted to be a Taoist monk. He both loved the Asian Chinese philosophy and I Ching. And he also loves technology. So the deep seek moment was the moment where he believes that he can meaningfully combine the two things together and create his company, which is AI Fortune Telling.
turns.zh: 是啊，可惜。我见到了——对，一款叫 FateTel 的 AI 占星 app 的创始人。他这个人，10 年前想当道士。他既热爱中国传统的亚洲哲学和《易经》，也热爱科技。所以 DeepSeek 时刻对他来说，是他相信自己可以把这两样东西有意义地结合起来、创办自己公司的那一刻，也就是 AI 算命。

turns.en: How common is it for like, someone from an Alibaba or a Tencent to go to this town, which I think I've been to actually on the way to Guangdong like ages ago to see the mountains, but I can't remember. How usual is it? Like, do people recruit from there or try to recruit vibe coders in the same way that like we have an intense competition for engineers here in the U.S. and people, you know, they trade them like baseball stars with like salaries to match kind of. Do you see the same thing happening in China or not really?
turns.zh: 像 Alibaba 或 Tencent（腾讯）的人跑去这个小镇，这种情况有多普遍？我其实觉得我去过那个地方，很久以前在去广东的路上，去看山，但我记不清了。这种事儿常见吗？比如，人们会从那儿招人，或者试图招募 vibe coder，就像我们在美国这边对工程师的激烈争夺那样——人们像交易棒球明星一样把他们换来换去、配上匹配的薪资。你在中国看到同样的情况吗，还是并不？

turns.en: I don't think in Liangzhou that's the case. I think in Liangzhou, it is more like people hear about lures about this place. People hear about really great living experience in this place. So many people just decide to just decide to go. I'm talking about like not talking about those high earning top AI researchers. Those are the people who actually don't want to do that. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得在良渚不是这样。在良渚，更多的是人们听到关于这个地方的种种好处，听到在这里生活的体验很棒，所以很多人就决定直接去。我说的不是那些高收入的顶尖 AI 研究员，那些人其实并不想去。是的。

turns.en: So this is really interesting because it sounds like at least for some people, AI in China is like intertwined with the potential for independence and autonomy and you can start your own business and make a living like in your own living room by developing a fortune telling app or whatever. Whereas in the U.S., there's like a sense of complete loss of control for a lot of people where it's just like this is going to make my life worse and there's nothing I can do about it.
turns.zh: 这真的很有意思，因为听起来至少对一些人来说，在中国的 AI 与获得独立和自主的可能性交织在一起——你可以在自己的客厅里，靠开发一款算命 app 之类的东西创业谋生。而在美国，很多人有一种彻底失去掌控的感觉，就好像这只会让我的生活更糟，而我对此无能为力。

turns.en: Yeah, I think AI today, like at least for a lot of young people, they still see this as a meaningful way for upward mobility. the job market is pretty harsh. And the majority of the resource and the capital are controlled by the term called laodeng, which means this older generation of people. So many young people really see AI as a meaningful way to sort of fight back or even revenge. And the reason why young people hop on this AI bus is because there's not much social mobility in China anymore. I think previously, If there is a social contract where, you know, you work really hard and you can make a lot of money, I think this equation starts to dissolve after COVID because of the economic downturn.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得今天的 AI，至少对很多年轻人来说，他们仍然把它看作一条有意义的向上流动的路径。就业市场相当残酷，绝大多数资源和资本都掌握在一个叫“老登”（laodeng）的群体手里，也就是老一辈的人。所以很多年轻人真的把 AI 看作一种有意义的反击、甚至复仇的方式。年轻人之所以跳上这趟 AI 快车，是因为中国的社会流动性已经不太多了。我觉得以前有一种社会契约，就是你努力工作就能赚很多钱，而这个等式在疫情之后因为经济下行开始瓦解了。

turns.en: Well, what's the youth unemployment right now is like almost 20 percent or something?
turns.zh: 那么，现在的青年失业率大概是多少？接近 20% 左右？

turns.en: Yeah, the official number is 18.9 percent. And it is usually this number is I would cast some doubt.
turns.zh: 是的，官方数字是 18.9%。通常这个数字，我会持一些怀疑。

turns.en: So I want to talk about this more, the perception of AI as an opportunity, because in the U.S. there are a lot of the same concerns about, okay, social mobility, it isn't what it used to be, et cetera. The previous generation holds all the wealth. Well, we hear that too, you know, like people complain about the boomer generation. But the view then is now AI. Is going to finally like kill us for good and lift up the ladder, right? So you imagine a law firm, we no longer need to hire junior partners. Imagine a investment bank, we no longer have to hire junior analysts. And the fear is not, or the view of AI is not that it's going to be an opportunity to like break out of some bad pattern, that it's going to be this lifting up of the ladders and that there is a generation, particularly young people, Maybe in college right now, maybe just graduated. It's like, oh, like AI is like foreclosing my future. And so I'm curious, like from the setting aside the vibe coding capital, but from someone who is like a young grad, why would they not look at AI and see the same thing that it's like, wow, like I studied or whatever. And now I will like deprive me of my like purpose for like being able to use my brain or get an entry level job or something like that.
turns.zh: 我想多聊聊这个——把 AI 视为一种机会的看法。因为在美国也有很多同样的担忧，比如社会流动性大不如前，等等。上一代人掌握了所有财富，这个我们也听得到，人们会抱怨婴儿潮一代（boomer）。但那时美国的看法是，AI 现在终于要彻底把我们干掉、把梯子抽走，对吧？你想想一家律所，我们不再需要雇佣初级合伙人了；你想想一家投行，我们不再需要雇佣初级分析师了。那种恐惧——或者说对 AI 的看法——不是它会成为一个打破糟糕模式的机会，而是它会把梯子抽走，让某一代人，尤其是年轻人，也许正在上大学、也许刚毕业，会觉得“哦，AI 在断送我的未来”。所以我很好奇，先撇开 vibe coding 之都不谈，就从一个年轻毕业生的角度看，他们为什么不会看着 AI 也得出同样的结论——就是“哇，我学了这么久，现在它却要剥夺我用大脑的意义、剥夺我找到入门级工作的机会”之类的？

turns.en: I think this dread exists in China as well. It is a consensus that many occupations and many majors offered in university will no longer be meaningful. But still, I do think Chinese people are cynical about education. This is why I got myself into investigating this AI education industry in China.
turns.zh: 我觉得这种恐惧在中国也存在。有一种共识是，很多职业、很多大学里开设的专业将不再有意义。但即便如此，我确实认为中国人对教育依然放不下。这也是为什么我会去调查中国的 AI 教育产业。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.en: What's that all about?
turns.zh: 那到底是怎么回事？

turns.en: So I went to this Liangzhu vibe coding town and the one core question I went, I want them to answer is how much money you can actually make with your vibe coding projects. And then not many people are actually doing, actually building a profitable business like that AI fortune telling company. Many vibe coders told me that they make money by selling AI classes. I was like, what do you mean by selling AI classes? And then I realized. It is a vast and unregulated and sort of lucrative industry that's just new and just out there.
turns.zh: 我去了良渚这个 vibe coding 小镇，我想让他们回答的一个核心问题是：靠你的 vibe coding 项目到底能赚多少钱。结果并没有多少人真的在靠做产品建立起一门赚钱的生意，像那个 AI 算命公司那样。很多 vibe coder 告诉我，他们靠卖 AI 课程赚钱。我就问，卖 AI 课程是什么意思？然后我意识到，这是一个庞大、缺乏监管、又相当赚钱的行业，全新，就摆在那儿。

turns.en: When I hear selling AI classes, by the way, I hear preying on people's fears. That here is this thing that's going to take off and you better learn how to use these things and pay me some money because otherwise you're going to be left behind.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我一听到“卖 AI 课程”，我听到的就是在利用人们的恐惧。就是说，有这么个东西要火起来了，你最好学会怎么用它们，然后付我点钱，否则你就要被落下了。

turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So after learning about this, I started to discover many more AI classes that's filled different corners of the Chinese internet from classes named from Deep Seek 101 to, you know, how to get rich with AI to how to AIGC 101. You know, all those classes are out there. So I went to this one company, which is branded as one of the largest AI education company in China. The company's name is peculiar. It's called Shengcai Youshu. The literal translation is there is an art of getting rich. So it was situated in Hangzhou Future Tech City, very close to the Alibaba's headquarter. I was taken by an AI influencer, his name is Mr. Tree, to the company. It was on 26th floor in a beautiful office building where I can just like see the entire Hangzhou city. And the theme color of this company is green. It's the color of dollars. And then they actually do offer a class called Use AI to Make Dollars. So this is a sort of company that provides hundreds of AI classes to people, and they have 80,000 paying members. When you become a paid member, you're encouraged to write more promotional text to recruit new members.
turns.zh: 是的，完全没错。了解到这一点之后，我开始发现更多充斥在中国互联网各个角落的 AI 课程，从叫“DeepSeek 101”的课，到“如何用 AI 致富”，再到“AIGC 101”。这些课程到处都是。我去了其中一家公司，它被标榜为中国最大的 AI 教育公司之一。这家公司的名字很特别，叫“生财有术”（Shengcai Youshu），字面意思是“致富是有门道的”。它坐落在杭州未来科技城，离 Alibaba 总部很近。一位 AI 网红带我去了这家公司，他叫“Tree 先生”（Mr. Tree）。公司在一栋漂亮写字楼的 26 层，在那儿我能俯瞰整个杭州城。这家公司的主色调是绿色，美元的颜色。他们还真开了一门课叫“用 AI 赚美元”。所以这是一家向人们提供数百门 AI 课程的公司，他们有 8 万名付费会员。当你成为付费会员后，你会被鼓励写更多推广文案去招募新会员。

turns.en: So this is an MLM kind of thing.
turns.zh: 所以这是那种传销（MLM，多层次营销）式的东西。

turns.en: It's MLM. It is MLM. Okay, yeah. So I was introduced to this company. I was introduced to this whole almost like a pyramid scheme of this company. And I realized that the nature of this company is actually selling people opportunity or selling people some hope. If you are a paid member, you have access to all sorts of classes and other paid members. And there's an interesting way you can sort of upgrade yourself in this pyramid. you're encouraged to collect something called Dragon Ball. If you collect enough Dragon Ball, then you will upgrade yourself from the Voyager level to the Deep Sea Circle.
turns.zh: 是传销，就是传销。好，是的。我被引荐进了这家公司，被引荐进这个几乎像金字塔骗局的体系。我意识到，这家公司的本质其实是在向人们贩卖机会，或者说贩卖希望。如果你是付费会员，你就能接触到各种课程和其他付费会员。有一种很有意思的方式可以让你在这个金字塔里往上升级：你会被鼓励去收集一种叫“龙珠”（Dragon Ball）的东西。如果你收集到足够的龙珠，你就会从“航海者”（Voyager）级别升级到“深海圈”（Deep Sea Circle）。

turns.en: Do you get an actual Dragon Ball thing or just points assigned to you?
turns.zh: 你会得到一个真的龙珠物件，还是只是给你记一些积分？

turns.en: They have some native apps developed in them, and then I think it is some sort of thing you can accumulate, but I guess they made it somewhat... adventurous and romantic Dragon Ball. Anyways, all the names are somewhat associated with adventure was like, you know, a voyage on the sea. So you can, yeah, you can just basically upgrade yourself and eventually you will be upgraded to the deep sea circle, which is a CEO circle where the high value people are forming this exclusive in real life clubs where you can participate. So I realized there are three kinds of people who are registering to be a paid member. By the way, the membership for this company is about 3,000, 4,000 yuan, which is half of average monthly salary in Hangzhou, which is not a cheap price. So the three kind of people who are the paid members are By my estimation, the first kind is the proper underdogs. What do I mean by underdogs? They're either just graduated from college with a degree that doesn't really give them meaningful prospect. Or there are some people who don't have a degree from elite universities. They just want to sort of like use AI to arm themselves. And the second kind of people who would pay for those classes, I would say, are the smaller manufacturers in China. They're the ones who are somewhat established, already have a running business. They want to use AI to improve their supply chains. They want to use AI to writing the Amazon listicles so they can sell their stuff to the overseas consumers. They want to use AI to meaningfully boost up their business. And the third kind are the people who are professional vibe coders. They need to be around like-minded people. They are, you know, the OPCs, the one-person companies. They're the ones who need an office space. So these are the people I encountered in this company, you know, the art of getting rich. It is a very strange place where the way they talk about AI is almost like alchemy. The founder himself is an Alibaba veteran. He quit his job and decided to, by his own claim, helping young people to gain dignity through learning. I think in a society like China where education and meritocracy is held as a near religious status, it is a very like a Confucius and a very absurd scene to be in.
turns.zh: 他们内部开发了一些原生 app，我觉得那是某种你可以累积的东西，但我猜他们把它做得多少有点……冒险和浪漫色彩的“龙珠”。总之，所有的名字都跟冒险有点关联，像是海上航行那种。所以你可以，对，基本上就是不断给自己升级，最终你会升到“深海圈”，那是一个 CEO 圈子，那些高价值的人组成这种线下的、排他的俱乐部，你可以参加。所以我发现有三类人会注册成为付费会员。顺便说一下，这家公司的会员费大约 3000 到 4000 元，相当于杭州平均月薪的一半，价格不便宜。据我估计，这三类付费会员是：第一类是真正的“弱势者”（underdog）。什么叫弱势者？他们要么是刚大学毕业、拿着一个并不能带来有意义前景的学位，要么是那些没有名校学历的人，他们只想用 AI 来武装自己。第二类会付费上课的人，我觉得是中国的小型制造商。他们已经有点根基、有正在运营的生意，想用 AI 改进供应链，想用 AI 来写 Amazon 的商品清单文案，好把货卖给海外消费者，想用 AI 有意义地提振自己的生意。第三类是职业 vibe coder，他们需要跟志同道合的人待在一起，他们是那些 OPC、一人公司，是需要办公空间的人。这些就是我在这家“生财有术”公司里遇到的人。那是个很奇怪的地方，他们谈论 AI 的方式几乎像在炼金术。创始人自己是 Alibaba 老兵，他辞了职，按他自己的说法，是要帮助年轻人通过学习获得尊严。我觉得在中国这样一个把教育和精英选拔（meritocracy）奉为近乎宗教地位的社会里，这是一个非常儒家、又非常荒诞的场景。

turns.en: Yeah, I was going to say China also has a history of going through these sort of predatory educational waves, I guess, like with English teachers and then all the like for-profit private tutors, which was such a problem that the Chinese government ended up cracking down on that. A lot of them were VC funded.
turns.zh: 是啊，我正想说，中国也有一段经历这类掠夺性教育浪潮的历史，我想，比如英语老师，然后是各种营利的私教，那问题大到中国政府最后出手打压。他们很多都是拿了 VC（风投）的钱的。

turns.en: Oh, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，是的。

turns.en: And the Chinese government ended up cracking down on them, I guess, in, was it 2021?
turns.zh: 中国政府最后打压了他们，我记得是 2021 年吧？

turns.en: Yeah, I can't remember anymore. But speaking of that, actually, so this raises kind of a question of, I guess... cyclical overcapacity. We see this also time and time again in China, which is the government says like, okay, we don't want you to put money in for-profit educational firms anymore. We don't want you to put all your money in internet companies. We want you to start putting money into semiconductor manufacturing, or I guess what we would call hard tech. And then what happens is we have an explosion in supply and everyone starts competing on price to the death. And then the whole area gets sort of like cleansed out at one point. When you look at AI right now, is there a danger that we're just going to end up with this bloated like vibe coding sector of apps and slot videos that like don't actually make any money and don't actually lead to any technological progress?
turns.zh: 是啊，我记不清了。不过说到这个，其实这就引出了一个我想是“周期性产能过剩”的问题。我们在中国一次又一次地看到这个：政府说，好，我们不希望你们再把钱投进营利的教育公司了，不希望你们把钱都投进互联网公司了，我们希望你们开始把钱投进半导体制造，或者我们称之为“硬科技”（hard tech）的东西。然后发生的是，供给大爆发，每个人都开始拼价格、拼到你死我活，最后整个领域在某个时点被清洗出去。当你现在看 AI，有没有一种危险：我们最后只会得到一个臃肿的 vibe coding 板块，全是 app 和老虎机式的视频，实际上并不赚钱、也并不带来任何技术进步？

turns.en: And just to add on, like other 900 other fortune telling apps that you did that didn't get written about.
turns.zh: 再补一句，还有另外 900 个你做了、但没被写进报道的算命 app。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: Because you know what I'm saying?
turns.zh: 因为你懂我意思吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, that's a great question. When I was in Liangzhou, there are a lot of entrepreneurs. They are the ones who claim themselves to build something meaningful. But when I asked them, how many users you have? Three, seven, eight.
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊，这是个好问题。我在良渚的时候，有很多创业者，他们都声称自己在做有意义的东西。但当我问他们，你有多少用户？三个、七个、八个。

turns.en: It's like when people say they're micro-influencers.
turns.zh: 就像有人说自己是“微型网红”（micro-influencer）那样。

turns.en: Yeah, right, right.
turns.zh: 是啊，对，对。

turns.en: So there are just really a lot of people who claim to build things. And then at the same time, they're like filling app stores with applications with information. single-digit users, there are probably five to ten other companies are building astrology apps or fortune-telling apps in Liangzhou, just in this town. And the fattest tale, it is the story I told in my New Yorker piece, is the only one that's profitable. And the reason why I got into the story of fattest tale, this AI storytelling.
turns.zh: 所以真的有太多人声称自己在做东西。与此同时，他们在往应用商店里塞满各种应用，用户数只有个位数。光在良渚这一个小镇，可能就有五到十家别的公司也在做占星 app 或算命 app。而其中唯一赚钱的，就是我在 New Yorker 文章里讲的那个 FateTel。我之所以会介入 FateTel 这个 AI 讲故事……

turns.en: App, is because.
turns.zh: ……app 的故事，是因为。

turns.en: The founder wanted me to be in his office opening party. It's because I am seen as someone who can bring prosperity to them. Because in my body's astrology, I process a lot of fire. And his body's astrology process a lot of water. So my presence in the office opening party can be seen as balance the room's energy. You got to.
turns.zh: 创始人想让我出席他的办公室开业派对。这是因为我被看作一个能给他们带来财运的人。因为按我八字（Bazi）的命理，我命中带很多“火”，而他的八字带很多“水”。所以我出现在开业派对上，可以被看作是在平衡这个房间的能量。你得……

turns.en: Balance the room's energy.
turns.zh: 平衡房间的能量。

turns.en: I'm metal. Is that good for fire?
turns.zh: 我是“金”。那对“火”好吗？

turns.en: You know, when I was in China, I was sort of sick. I was like, I had like a stomachache that day. And the guy who was taking me around, he's like, I can take you to like a traditional Chinese doctor. And I was like, come on, you don't like really believe in that stuff, do you? And he was like, well, there's like 1.5 billion of us. So maybe you should, maybe you should consider that we might know a little bit of something about surviving. That's kind of now how I feel about when I hear like this astrology stuff. It's like, It all seems like nonsense to me, but more Chinese than anyone else. Maybe there's something I don't know about some of the wisdom here.
turns.zh: 你知道，我在中国的时候有点不舒服，那天我肚子疼。带我四处转的那个人说，我可以带你去看个中医。我就说，得了吧，你不是真信这些东西吧，对吧？他说，嗯，我们有 15 亿人，所以也许你应该考虑一下，关于怎么活下去这件事，我们可能多少懂点门道。这差不多就是我现在听到这些占星的东西时的感觉。就是，这些东西在我看来全都像无稽之谈，但中国人比任何人都多，也许这里面有些智慧是我所不了解的。

turns.en: A lot of feng shui principles are just like good decorating sense.
turns.zh: 很多风水（feng shui）原则其实就是好的装饰品味。

turns.en: Yeah, like maybe just empirically.
turns.zh: 是啊，也许只是经验上总结出来的。

turns.en: Like don't put your bed directly opposite a door because that's just freaky. That makes sense.
turns.zh: 比如别把床正对着门，因为那样就是很瘆人。这说得通。

turns.en: It's hard for me to imagine that you could achieve prosperity by getting the balance of water and fire energy in the room, right? But again, look at the scoreboard. There's a lot more Chinese than the rest of us. And so maybe that tells you something about just sort of following the ancient wisdom.
turns.zh: 我很难想象，你可以通过平衡房间里水和火的能量来获得财运，对吧？但话说回来，看看记分牌：中国人比我们其他所有人加起来都多，所以也许这本身就说明了，遵循那些古老的智慧是有点道理的。

turns.en: Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 是啊，对。

turns.en: So it was a really.
turns.zh: 所以那真是一个……

turns.en: Yeah, it was indeed.
turns.zh: 是啊，确实是。

turns.en: A very absurd experience because China... has been witnessing this revival of new agey practice or astrological practice after COVID. I do think many more people started to feel like they can't really get a hold on life. A lot of things don't make sense anymore. The economy started to stall and the real estate market bursted. So many people turn into astrologers because they want some sort of certainty in life. They want some interpretability in life. So that's why it became a really lucrative industry in China. I mean, right after DeepSeek came out, one of the most popular way of communicating with DeepSeek was let DeepSeek to calculate your Chinese astrology and have DeepSeek to sort of guide you through a lot of challenges based on your Chinese bads astrology. And the success of a company like Figtail is not singular. And the way that entire Fatal company is basically revolved around the Bazaar astrology itself, like all the employees, they did Bazaar compatibility before being hired or before hiring others. And they're really serious about this thing.
turns.zh: ……非常荒诞的经历，因为中国在疫情之后一直见证着这种新时代（new age）修行或占星修行的复兴。我确实觉得，越来越多的人开始感到自己抓不住生活了，很多事情不再讲得通，经济开始停滞，房地产市场崩了。所以很多人转向占星，因为他们想要生活中的某种确定性，想要某种可解释性。这就是为什么它在中国成了一门非常赚钱的生意。我是说，DeepSeek 出来之后，最流行的跟它交流的方式之一，就是让 DeepSeek 帮你算八字，让它根据你的中国八字命理来引导你度过很多难题。像 FateTel 这样一家公司的成功并不是个例。整个 FateTel 公司基本上就是围绕八字本身运转的，比如所有员工在被录用之前、或在招人之前，都会做八字配对。他们对这件事非常认真。

turns.en: I used to know a banker in Hong Kong, and she had an app. That would tell her like her fortune every day, as well as her lucky color. And then she would religiously dress head to toe in this one color. If it was purple or black or yellow, she would just wear all of that.
turns.zh: 我以前认识香港的一位银行家，她有个 app，每天会告诉她她的运势，还有她的幸运色。然后她会虔诚地从头到脚穿成那一种颜色。如果那天是紫色、黑色或黄色，她就全身都穿那个颜色。

turns.en: Yeah, it is interesting phenomenon. People are serious about this. I'm not joking. When I was visiting this vibe cone in capital Liangzhu, when I see the official calendar, you have a municipal official calendar. A lot of the public events are teaching people how to dress for luck. According to the Chinese astrological calendar, a lot of practices are being revered as serious.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个很有意思的现象，人们对此很认真，我不是在开玩笑。我去良渚这个 vibe coding 之都探访时，看到官方日历——就是市政的官方日历——很多公共活动都在教人们怎么穿衣才能招好运。按照中国占星历法，很多做法都被当作严肃的事情来尊崇。

turns.en: I think I need to. How do you pronounce it? Yeah, the four pillars of destiny. I need to figure out my four pillars of destiny.
turns.zh: 我觉得我得……这个怎么念？对，“四柱命理”（four pillars of destiny，即八字）。我得算算我自己的四柱命理。

turns.en: This is what I'm saying.
turns.zh: 我说的就是这个意思。

turns.en: It sounds weird to look at an app and say, I'm going to dress in all yellow today. But if you're succeeding or whatever, then who am I to question? But this also gets to something at the founding of the People's Republic of China. And Mao talked about like socialism with Chinese characteristics. And I heard that term a bunch when I was younger. And I didn't know what that meant. That term, that part with Chinese characteristics. And I sort of wondered when I'm reading your reporting that. whether part of the reason why the public in China does not have the same negative view towards development as maybe it has in the U.S. is because it's something high tech with Chinese characteristics. That basically, yes, the world has changed multiple times. The world is changing again. The world is changing again. These cities don't look anything like they did at some point. For a lot of people, it's a very disorienting experience. But the through line is that some Chinese characteristics have remained and it's like high tech with sharing Chinese characteristics and that it feels like comfortable in a way that development in the U.S. does not. Where in development in the U.S. feels like it destroys culture rather than modernizes it.
turns.zh: 看着一个 app 然后说“我今天要全身穿黄色”，这听起来很怪。但如果你因此过得顺风顺水，那我又凭什么去质疑呢？不过这也牵扯到中华人民共和国建国时的一些东西。毛泽东谈到过“有中国特色的社会主义”。我小时候常听到这个词，但我不知道它是什么意思，就是“有中国特色”那部分。我在读你的报道时有点琢磨：中国公众之所以不像美国那样对发展持同样的负面看法，一部分原因是不是因为这是一种“有中国特色的高科技”。基本上，是的，世界已经改变了很多次，世界又在改变，这些城市跟它们过去的样子已经完全不同了。对很多人来说，这是一种非常令人迷失方向的体验。但那条贯穿始终的主线是，一些“中国特色”保留了下来，这就像是一种“有中国特色的高科技”，它让人感觉舒适，而这是美国的发展所没有的。在美国，发展感觉像是在摧毁文化，而不是让文化现代化。

turns.en: I would say maybe something like, something like Asian practices, like the traditional Chinese medicine and baths, like my ground people spiritually, like I was talking to you, this Canadian reporter, Ian Johnson, he was telling me that the reason why people turn into BaZi is because it is a study practice that has been existing for thousands of years. And then today, there's a lot of unpredictabilities in today's world. And going to BaZi seems to Explain something in a metaphysical sense as the today's Chinese young people are going into this phase where you have a material abundance already. And then you need to go inward and to seek certain spiritual meanings. I think that aspect exists. But also I would argue that the rapid Chinese industrialization and urbanization and development actually was very psychologically disoriental for many Chinese people. I do think a common psychological experience that people experienced in the past many years is this utterly like dislocation of one's root. There's a writer, Yanlian Ke. He wrote about this little rural village sort of within a few decades growing to a giant metropolis. And then the novel itself is called the Explosion Chronicles. It is a fake historical account of a town story. And then like, all those characters in this fiction are experiencing this collective psychosis. It's because the Asian to the traditional custom, how people identify each other, how people build relationship with each other, all sort of dismantled by this rapid industrialization. And then in the past, people are always saying China is going too fast and people cannot catch up. And I do think this is a very, well, like a common experience for many people.
turns.zh: 我会说，也许是像亚洲的这些传统修行，比如中医和八字，在精神上给我的族人一种根基感。就像我跟你说的，那位加拿大记者 Ian Johnson（易明）告诉我，人们之所以转向八字，是因为它是一门已经存在了几千年的修行学问。而今天的世界里有很多不确定性，去求八字似乎能在形而上的意义上解释一些东西。如今的中国年轻人正处在这样一个阶段：你已经拥有了物质上的丰裕，然后你需要向内走，去寻找某种精神上的意义。我觉得这个层面是存在的。但同时我也要指出，中国快速的工业化、城市化和开发，其实让很多中国人在心理上非常迷失。我确实觉得，过去这些年人们经历的一种共同心理体验，就是这种根被彻底拔起的错位感。有位作家阎连科（Yan Lianke），他写过一个小小的农村在几十年间成长为一座巨型都市的故事。那部小说本身叫《爆炸纪事》（The Explosion Chronicles，音），是一个虚构的、伪历史式的乡镇故事。小说里所有的人物都在经历这种集体性的精神错乱。这是因为对传统习俗的依附——人们如何彼此认同、如何彼此建立关系——全都被这种快速的工业化瓦解了。过去人们总说，中国走得太快，人们跟不上。我确实觉得这是很多人的一种共同体验。

turns.en: Is China, would you still describe China as a high trust society? No. Really?
turns.zh: 中国——你还会把中国描述成一个高信任社会吗？不会？真的？

turns.en: I wouldn't.
turns.zh: 我不会这么说。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Because it feels like part of the problem in the U.S. is we have shifted into a very low-trust society. And so when you hear people say, oh, AI is going to create a utopia, the distrust is automatically there because we've been through so much other technological change that a lot of people would say hasn't actually improved their lives. But in China, you think it's now a low-trust society because of COVID?
turns.zh: 因为感觉美国问题的一部分在于，我们已经转变成了一个非常低信任的社会。所以当你听到有人说“哦，AI 会创造一个乌托邦”，那种不信任是自动就有的，因为我们经历了太多其他的技术变革，很多人会说这些变革其实并没有改善他们的生活。但在中国，你觉得现在它成了低信任社会，是因为疫情吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I think it's a low-trust society. Post-COVID... China become more zero-sum. The civil servant examination is one of the popular examination that selects brilliant people into the Chinese bureaucratic system. And then many people would sort of fight each other for a spot with a very dark foresty logic. Like dark forest is a term coined by Liu Cixin, the sci-fi writer who wrote Three-Body Problems. And people constantly using dark forest to describe their day-to-day reality in China. If they successfully get a spot in the civil servant examination, they might get reported or somewhat people get jealous. Essentially, it's because opportunities are getting less and less and then people are have developed a much more zero-sum mindset.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得它是个低信任社会。疫情之后，中国变得更零和了。公务员考试是最受欢迎的考试之一，它把优秀的人选拔进中国的官僚体系。很多人会用一种非常“黑暗森林”式的逻辑去争抢一个名额。“黑暗森林”（dark forest）是科幻作家刘慈欣（Liu Cixin，《三体》的作者）造的一个词。人们不停地用“黑暗森林”来形容他们在中国的日常生活现实。如果他们成功考上了一个公务员名额，可能会被举报，或者招来别人的嫉妒。归根结底，是因为机会越来越少，人们养成了一种更加零和的心态。

turns.en: But then how do we square? There's still this drive towards meritocracy or this belief that if I work really hard and I get a good education, it's going to pay off at some point. And yet the opportunities are getting smaller. Why are people even trying anymore? Yeah, that's a great question.
turns.zh: 但我们怎么把这解释圆呢？还是有这种对精英选拔的追逐，或者说这种信念：只要我非常努力、接受好的教育，它总会在某个时点得到回报。可机会却在变得越来越小。人们为什么还在努力呢？是啊，这是个好问题。

turns.en: There's a lot of contradictions you cannot really reason away.
turns.zh: 有很多矛盾是你没法真正用逻辑解释掉的。

turns.en: I I guess it's their best option.
turns.zh: 我猜这是他们最好的选择。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Economists in the U.S. would say the U.S. is experiencing a K-shaped economy. You have an upward lag, which indicates the advancing technologies, the booming industry. You also have a downward lag. I think it's a very similar case in China. The upward lag is.
turns.zh: 美国的经济学家会说美国正在经历一种 K 型经济。你有一条向上的分支，代表着进步的技术、蓬勃的行业；你还有一条向下的分支。我觉得中国的情况非常类似。向上的那条分支是……

turns.en: And we did have the live flat movement. So some people have taken the other path.
turns.zh: 而且我们确实有过“躺平”（lie flat）运动。所以有些人走了另一条路。

turns.en: I feel lied to by the Chinese propagandists I talked to on Twitter and on Instagram. It's like everything is booming and, you know, it's like lifting all boats and stuff like that. And consumption is really well distributed. But you said something at the beginning that sort of relates to this. You're like prior to deep sea. That there was this, I guess, anxiety on the part of Chinese tech about, well, what do we have?
turns.zh: 我觉得被我在 Twitter 和 Instagram 上关注的那些中国宣传者骗了。感觉就像什么都在蓬勃增长，你知道，就像“水涨众船高”那样，消费也分配得很均匀。但你在开头说的某件事跟这个有点关系。你说，在 DeepSeek 之前，中国科技界有一种焦虑，就是“那我们又有什么呢？”

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But in 2022 and 2023, we were doing a bunch of like episodes with our jaws dropped about, oh, advances in batteries, advances in cars, maybe like all of the industrial advances. And that's still the case, right? There's still these extraordinary leap forward things. I don't mean to like literally, that was an accident. You just leap forward in that context, but literally leap forwards in like sort of manufacturing capabilities, et cetera. The car export number is enormous. Pretty soon, one day, maybe all cars will be made in China. How does that fit into this idea or a self-conception of stagnation?
turns.zh: 但在 2022 和 2023 年，我们做了一大堆让我们惊掉下巴的节目，讲哦，电池的进步、汽车的进步，也许还有各种工业上的进步。而现在依然如此，对吧？还是有这些非凡的“大跃进”式的东西。我不是要字面地那么说——那是个意外——你就是在那个语境里“跃进”了一下，但真的是制造业能力等方面的跃进。汽车出口数字非常庞大。也许很快有一天，所有的车都会在中国制造。这又怎么契合那种停滞的自我认知呢？

turns.en: I don't want to destroy your China maxing moment. I don't deny that if you go to a place like Shenzhen, you can really experience a futuristic ecological civilization. Those cities are absolutely beautiful. China is absolutely, it does viscerally feel more optimistic and futuristic than the majority of American cities. You know, you have Chongqing, you have those cyberpunk cities. But at the same time, I want to faithfully translate the percentage of people's anxiety and the percentage of people's optimism into my reporting.
turns.zh: 我不想毁掉你的“China maxing”时刻。我不否认，如果你去深圳这样的地方，你真的能体验到一种未来感的生态文明。那些城市美得不得了。中国绝对——它确实在直觉上比大多数美国城市更乐观、更有未来感。你有重庆，你有那些赛博朋克（cyberpunk）式的城市。但同时，我想在我的报道里忠实地把人们焦虑的比例和人们乐观的比例都翻译出来。

turns.en: No, this is why it's real reporting and not just me sharing a TikTok.
turns.zh: 不，这正是为什么这是真正的报道，而不只是我分享一个 TikTok。

turns.en: Yeah, so when you have futuristic cities, when you have something like high-speed rail, for example, connecting a lot of metropolises in China, 85% I think 80 to 85% of those high-speed rails are losing money. So this is the grim reality where on the surface, China seems to be in prosperity. It's booming, but people day to day, they are relatively struggling. My experience is if you go to China, you'll realize people's income hasn't really changed or increased compared to 10 years ago. People are less likely to spend compared to 10 years ago. People do not really want to invest their money into the stock market because you will end up losing a lot of money. People did put their money into the real estate market, and then people at the end lost the money. So this is like many cases that happen in China. And then again, young people are struggling to find jobs. And today's China is really like, it's a different China, if you're talking about it, from 10, 15 years ago. Today's China is much of a, Japanified China. It resembles to Japan's stalled economy. And the young people sentiment resembles to Japanese young people. You have a sense of material abundance. You have a sense of comfort life. At the same time, there's not much growth opportunities for individuals. And at the same time, AI industries is a highly selective and concentrated industry. If you don't have a degree from a Qinghua Yao class, for example, it's harder for you to get those one-off lucrative offers from a top AI company.
turns.zh: 是的。所以当你有未来感的城市，当你有像高铁这样连接中国很多大都市的东西时——我觉得高铁里有 85%、大概 80% 到 85% 都是亏钱的。所以这就是那个严峻的现实：表面上看，中国似乎一片繁荣、欣欣向荣，但人们日常其实是相对挣扎的。我的体验是，如果你去中国，你会发现人们的收入跟 10 年前相比其实没什么变化或增长。人们比 10 年前更不愿意消费。人们不太想把钱投进股市，因为最后你会亏很多钱。人们确实把钱投进了房地产市场，然后最后也亏了。所以这是在中国发生的很多情况。再一次，年轻人在挣扎着找工作。今天的中国，如果你要谈论它的话，跟 10 年、15 年前已经是一个不同的中国了。今天的中国很大程度上是一个“日本化”（Japanified）的中国，它类似于日本停滞的经济，年轻人的心态也类似于日本的年轻人。你有一种物质丰裕的感觉，有一种生活舒适的感觉，但同时，个人没有太多成长机会。而且 AI 行业是一个高度挑剔、高度集中的行业。如果你没有清华“姚班”（Qinghua Yao class）那样的学位，你就更难拿到顶尖 AI 公司那种一次性的高薪 offer。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit more about the micro dramas and AI slop and where they come from? Because as you describe it in your piece, it's sort of like if Detroit, I guess, nowadays became like this giant AI slop factory.
turns.zh: 你能再多谈谈那些微短剧（micro drama）和 AI slop，以及它们是从哪儿来的吗？因为就像你在文章里描述的，那感觉就好像，我想，如今的底特律（Detroit）变成了一个巨型的 AI slop 工厂。

turns.en: Yeah, I really wanted to write a techno-optimistic story about AI slop.
turns.zh: 是的，我真的很想写一个关于 AI slop 的技术乐观主义故事。

turns.en: It's a noble goal.
turns.zh: 这是个崇高的目标。

turns.en: Yeah, it's a noble goal. The more I get into the story, the more people I talk to, the more I realize that it could be an illusion because people have been telling me the Chinese vertical AI dramas could be a real tool for China to export soft power. It could be a real Chinese innovation. So really, I was hoping to find more innovative or creative stories to write about. But later I discovered that China has already established what I call the industrial slop complex. It is a result of many factors. One of the factors is many local governments, they are in the stage of being very risk averse. So they want to put the money and effort into strategic sectors, a strategic industry, and AI has been seen as a strategic industry. So all the local governments are trying to show to Beijing that we're putting the technological priority into our region.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个崇高的目标。可我越深入这个故事、跟越多人聊，就越意识到那可能是一种幻觉。因为人们一直告诉我，中国的垂直 AI 短剧可能成为中国输出软实力的一个真正的工具，可能是一项真正的中国创新。所以我真的很希望能找到更多有创新性或创造性的故事来写。但后来我发现，中国已经建立起了我称之为“工业 slop 综合体”（industrial slop complex）的东西。这是很多因素造成的结果。其中一个因素是，很多地方政府正处在一个非常规避风险的阶段，所以它们想把钱和精力投进战略性行业，而 AI 一直被视为战略性产业。于是所有地方政府都在努力向北京展示：我们正在把科技优先落地到我们这个区域。

turns.en: Showing them literally with videos, right? Because they're sort of like easy to make. Yeah, look what we made.
turns.zh: 而且是用视频实打实地展示给他们看，对吧？因为视频比较好做。“瞧，看我们做了什么。”

turns.en: Exactly. And then AIGC, AI content generated, AI generated video is the lowest bar to enter this AI as a strategic industry. So you see many cities like Qingdao, Wuhan, Zhengzhou, those cities normally don't really associate themselves with tech. They're the ones jumping onto this AIGC bandwagon the fastest.
turns.zh: 正是如此。而 AIGC（AI 生成内容）、AI 生成的视频，是把 AI 当作战略性产业来切入的最低门槛。所以你会看到很多城市，比如青岛（Qingdao）、武汉（Wuhan）、郑州（Zhengzhou），这些城市平时并不太会把自己跟科技联系在一起，而它们却是跳上 AIGC 这股风潮最快的。

turns.en: This is very interesting because this is what people would say is one of the classic problems with certain top-down economic planning is like, guys, we really need to like have more AI. And then a bunch of regional leaders, it's like, all right, let's get that.
turns.zh: 这非常有意思，因为这就是人们会说的那种自上而下经济规划的经典问题之一：就是“各位，我们真的需要更多 AI”，然后一堆地方领导就说“好，那我们来搞这个”。

turns.en: Yeah, it's the overcapacity issue.
turns.zh: 是啊，这就是产能过剩的问题。

turns.en: Yeah, but also it's like, that's not really productive force AI in the way that building a new training advanced neural network or a chip is. So this region is like, we're going to be the slop factory. It's like, look, we're doing AI stuff.
turns.zh: 是啊，但还在于，这并不是真正意义上的“生产力”AI，不像训练一个先进神经网络或造一块芯片那样。所以这个区域就说“我们要当那个 slop 工厂”，就像“看，我们在做 AI 的东西”。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: That's what it sounds like.
turns.zh: 听起来就是那样。

turns.en: Absolutely. So on top of, you know, like Shenzhen, Wuhan or Qingdao or Zhengzhou, there's mental gold. There's a very distant district of Beijing is basically seen as the Staten Island of Beijing. And the mental gold government be like, we're going to attract. many AI talents to come to us. We're going to cultivate them to be the AIGC talents, and we're going to establish a flourishing AIGC industry. So this is the reality.
turns.zh: 完全正确。所以在深圳、武汉、青岛、郑州之外，还有门头沟（Mentougou）。那是北京一个很偏远的区，基本上被看作是北京的“Staten Island”（史坦顿岛，意指偏远的区）。门头沟政府的想法是：我们要吸引很多 AI 人才来我们这儿，我们要把他们培养成 AIGC 人才，我们要建立一个繁荣的 AIGC 产业。所以这就是现实。

turns.en: As Tracy said, though, there's a lot of demand for AI slop, so it just might work.
turns.zh: 不过正如 Tracy 说的，对 AI slop 的需求很大，所以它可能真能行得通。

turns.en: Is there?
turns.zh: 真有吗？

turns.en: I don't know.
turns.zh: 我不知道。

turns.en: You saw it on the subway. Yeah, but I don't see it every day on the subway. The reason I noticed it is because I was like, what is that thing that she's watching? It looks really weird.
turns.zh: 你是在地铁上看到的。是啊，但我不是每天在地铁上都能看到。我之所以注意到它，是因为我当时想，她看的那是个啥玩意儿？看起来特别怪。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, today's China is producing a lot of AIGC short dramas. I'm talking about there's a projection for next year and saying next year there will be five million those AI drama shows that can be disseminated through your app on your smartphone. And today, the industry is actually not doing really well. Like, we're already seeing the ghost city effect of the AIGC industry. It means the majority of the content or the dramas produced are not being watched. If you have a hit rate, because, you know, the short video industry is very power lolly. It's like only the top content are been seen by the majority of people, the reality is only, I think, 0.16% of those AIGC content are considered as hits. And only those hits can meaningfully bring some revenue. And today, like 90% of AIGC companies are actually losing money. And then it is a result of this overenthusiastic local government trying to do something with AI. and ended up creating a lot of ghost cities in terms of those AI dramas.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的。我是说，今天的中国在生产大量的 AIGC 短剧。我说的是，有一个对明年的预测，说明年将会有 500 万部这样的 AI 剧集，可以通过你智能手机上的 app 传播。而今天，这个行业其实做得并不好。我们已经看到了 AIGC 行业的“鬼城效应”（ghost city effect），意思是生产出来的大部分内容或剧集根本没人看。因为你知道，短视频行业是非常幂律（power law）分布的，只有头部的内容才会被大多数人看到。现实是，我觉得只有 0.16% 的 AIGC 内容算得上是爆款，也只有这些爆款才能有意义地带来一些收入。而今天，90% 的 AIGC 公司其实都在亏钱。这是那些过度热情的地方政府试图用 AI 做点事情的结果，最后在这些 AI 剧集上造出了很多“鬼城”。

turns.en: The moment I actually first really noticed some of the China AI generated videos was in the early days. of the Iran war when we had a lot of anti-US propaganda, right? And then people were talking about like, oh, AI is going to be a big component of future government propaganda and whoever gets like the most viral video out the fastest is going to win. But actually, it's slightly a tangential question, but it's related to this. Do you have a theory for why China has struggled to export, I guess, more cultural things like movies, music? I mean, we've seen Japan go through the J-pop era, K-pop, Korean films.
turns.zh: 我真正第一次注意到一些中国 AI 生成视频的时刻，是在伊朗战争（Iran war）的早期，当时有很多反美宣传，对吧？人们谈论说，哦，AI 将成为未来政府宣传的一个重要组成部分，谁能最快做出最爆的视频谁就赢。不过这其实是个有点跑题的问题，但跟这个话题相关：你有没有一个理论，来解释为什么中国一直难以输出更多文化产品，比如电影、音乐？我是说，我们看到日本经历了 J-pop 时代，还有 K-pop、韩国电影。

turns.en: My kids love Korean stuff, yeah.
turns.zh: 我的孩子们特别喜欢韩国的东西，是啊。

turns.en: And China seems to have really struggled with that.
turns.zh: 而中国在这件事上似乎一直很吃力。

turns.en: There's definitely one reason is living in a society where... There's a metaphor someone told me, which is as a content creator or as an artist in China, it's like walking in a dark room where there are 10 pieces of furniture you cannot touch. If you touch it, then you will die. So this is the reality of creating something in China. Given this mindset or experience, given the censorship mechanism, given there are just like many invisible lines out there, that could trigger something, some consequences. So I would say people in China are less creative now. You see a flattening effect of the Chinese creative industry. And I guess the second one is China really lacks a cultural engine like Hollywood. I think part of it is a deliberate choice. 20 years ago, during the peak of China's industrialization, there's a famous economist, I couldn't recall his name now, but he was saying the real power of China is not replicating iPhone or Steve Jobs or Hollywood or Grammys. Like, we shall never envy them. We shall build factories and melt iron and forge metals. You know, we shall.
turns.zh: 肯定有一个原因是，生活在一个……有人跟我讲过一个比喻：在中国当一名内容创作者或艺术家，就像在一个漆黑的房间里走动，房间里有 10 件你不能碰的家具，如果你碰了，你就会死。这就是在中国创作东西的现实。鉴于这种心态或经历，鉴于审查机制，鉴于外面就是有很多看不见的红线，可能会触发某种后果，所以我会说，中国人现在的创造力更低了。你会看到中国创意产业的一种“扁平化”效应。我想第二个原因是，中国真的很缺乏一个像好莱坞（Hollywood）那样的文化引擎。我觉得这部分是一个刻意的选择。20 年前，在中国工业化的顶峰时期，有一位著名的经济学家——我现在想不起他的名字了——他说，中国真正的力量不在于复制 iPhone、Steve Jobs、好莱坞或格莱美（Grammys）。我们绝不应该羡慕它们，我们应该去建工厂、去炼铁、去锻造金属。我们应该……

turns.en: It's always steel.
turns.zh: 永远是钢铁。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Like, forge steels. Like, we shall build. Like, this is where China's core strength lays. So I guess... boosting the entertainment industry, like exporting culture goods to the rest of the world hasn't really been China's strategic emphasis. I guess that's where we're living in the result of that strategic choice.
turns.zh: 是的，正是如此。就是锻造钢铁，我们应该去建设。这就是中国核心力量之所在。所以我想……发展娱乐业、向世界其他地方输出文化产品，一直不是中国的战略重点。我想我们现在就生活在那个战略选择的结果里。

turns.en: I've also heard people say that just unlike, say, Japan and Korea, that entertainment creators have a gigantic domestic market to sell to and that you could be very successful creating entertainment content without it. going to the globe and a different because it's the scale of that domestic audience is different anyway effer long thank you so much for coming on thank you for having me that was a fantastic conversation and i'm looking forward to reading more of your reporting thank you Tracy, I thought that was a really interesting conversation, a very rich conversation.
turns.zh: 我也听人说过，跟日本、韩国不一样，娱乐创作者有一个巨大的国内市场可以卖，所以你可以在不走向全球的情况下，靠创作娱乐内容就非常成功，因为那个国内受众的规模本来就不一样。总之，Aphra，非常感谢你来上节目。“谢谢你们邀请我。”那是一场很棒的对话，我很期待读到你更多的报道。谢谢你，Tracy，我觉得那是一场非常有意思、内容非常丰富的对话。

turns.en: Yeah, there was a lot there. I was really surprised to hear her describe China as a low-trust society now because that's like actually a pretty big shift. And it also has me thinking obviously about the COVID response, but also the various crackdowns that we saw around that same time, the tech crackdowns, the education crackdowns, the three red lines on property. And a lot of people at the time were saying that, like, this is going to be destabilizing for China, not just in terms of its economy, but also socially, because you're telling people that a lot of the things they relied on, this idea that, like, you can become very wealthy by starting an Internet company or you can become very wealthy by investing in a house. Like, suddenly that was kind of gone.
turns.zh: 是啊，里面信息量很大。我很惊讶听到她现在把中国描述成一个低信任社会，因为这其实是一个相当大的转变。这也让我自然想到了疫情应对，还有我们在那段时间前后看到的各种打压：科技打压、教育打压、房地产“三条红线”（three red lines）。当时很多人都在说，这对中国来说会是破坏稳定的，不只是在经济上，也在社会上，因为你在告诉人们，他们依赖的很多东西——比如“你可以靠创办一家互联网公司变得非常富有”，或者“你可以靠投资房产变得非常富有”——突然之间都没了。

turns.en: The way you put it, it's like it just does seem to be the case with the Chinese economy that there are certain stories that, that are tailors all the time, certain cycles that happen over and over and over again. What were you going to say?

turns.en: My favorite example of this is China's pork industry. So they had a big swine flu outbreak in sort of the mid 2010s or late 2010s. And so suddenly we have these pork companies that like the stock just went shooting up. A lot of them turned to industrial pig farming. And then like a year or two later, the problem was massive oversupply. And then all these new pork suppliers were going out of business. And actually, if you look at like the pork price, You can see that for a few years, it just goes like up and down, up and down. And so it kicked off this cycle that was actually very hard to break.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的一个例子是中国的猪肉产业。他们在 2010 年代中期或后期爆发了一场大的猪瘟（swine flu）。他们很多的猪肉供给被消灭掉了，这是个大问题，因为猪肉至今仍是中国的当家肉类。于是中国政府开始往猪肉公司砸钱。突然间我们就有了这些猪肉公司，股价蹭蹭往上涨。它们很多转向了工业化养猪。然后大概一两年后，问题变成了严重的供给过剩，所有这些新的猪肉供应商又开始倒闭。实际上，如果你看猪肉价格，你会发现有那么几年，它就是这样上上下下、上上下下。这就开启了一个其实很难打破的周期。

turns.en: Yeah, totally. And these cycles are very good, it seems like, for winning an export market, right?
